items.caption: Amends Charter: Portland residents decide 2% of city’s annual discretionary budget.
items.question: Should Portland create participatory budgeting program for residents to make binding decisions to spend 2% of city’s discretionary budget?

summary.text: If approved, the amended Charter would require the Council to allocate at least  2% of the city's discretionary ongoing expenses towards a participatory budgeting program.

citations.quote: require Council to allocate an amount equivalent to at least 2% of the city’s adopted General Fund discretionary ongoing expenses

summary.text: If approved, the program would be developed with input from an oversight committee of residents from all Council districts.

citations.quote: Developed with input from oversight committee, selected by a process determined by Council, of residents from all Council districts

summary.text: Would the program be open to any resident's funding proposals for citywide or district projects?

citations.quote: Open to any resident’s funding proposals for citywide or district projects

for.text: Supporters argue that Measure 26-267 establishes a participatory budgeting program to give Portlanders a direct say in how to spend $16 million annually.

citations.quote: Participatory budgeting lets people like you help decide how your City spends a small sum of money.
citations.filed_by: Edward Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX

citations.quote: create a participatory budgeting program, giving all Portlanders a direct say in how to spend $16 million each year
citations.filed_by: Edward Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX

citations.quote: Measure 26-267, Your 2 Cents PDX, would bring this process to the City of Portland and help rebuild trust and accountability over the city budget.
citations.filed_by: Edward Alexander Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX

filed_by: Edward Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX

for.text: Argument filed by Edward Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX: “Portlanders have lost trust in City Hall. Too much money has been misplaced or poorly managed”

citations.quote: Portlanders have lost trust in City Hall. Too much money has been misplaced or poorly managed
citations.filed_by: Edward Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX

citations.quote: Participatory budgeting takes public budgeting out into the community where people live and work.
citations.filed_by: Edward Alexander Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX

citations.quote: We need new solutions to increase transparency and accountability, provide opportunities for more meaningful public participation, and rebuild public trust.
citations.filed_by: Edward Alexander Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX

citations.quote: Restoring trust and fostering trustworthy government requires bottom up reform.
citations.filed_by: Edward Alexander Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX

filed_by: Edward Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX
Edward Alexander Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX

against.text: Argument filed by Bob Weinstein: “The proposal would amend Portland’s Charter to require the city to forever hand over at least 2% of discretionary spending — initially $16 million— to a participatory budgeting process, no matter what else the city needs.”

citations.quote: The proposal would amend Portland’s Charter to require the city to forever hand over at least 2% of discretionary spending — initially $16 million— to a participatory budgeting process, no matter what else the city needs.
Measure 26-267 would permanently remove at least $16 million every year from the same General Fund that pays for fire and emergency response.
citations.filed_by: Isaac McLennan, President, Portland Firefighters’ Association, IAFF Local 43

citations.quote: This measure would permanently divert at least $16 million every year — written into the city charter, forever — out of the same General Fund that pays for firefighting, parks, community centers, Portland Street Response, and homeless services.
citations.filed_by: Laurie Wimmer, NW Oregon Labor Council

citations.quote: $16 million can fund more than 100 police officers. But once this amendment is in the charter, no future council can adjust it — not during a crime wave, not during a recession, not when federal funding disappears.
citations.filed_by: Sgt. Aaron Schmautz, Portland Police Association

filed_by: Isaac McLennan, President, Portland Firefighters’ Association, IAFF Local 43
Laurie Wimmer, NW Oregon Labor Council
Sgt. Aaron Schmautz, Portland Police Association

against.text: Argument filed by Jason Williams, Taxpayers Association of Oregon: “#3. Unelected Committees Make Binding Decisions An unelected “oversight committee” and “budget delegates” — not the elected Mayor or Council — assess, refine, and advance spending proposals to a binding vote.”

citations.quote: #3. Unelected Committees Make Binding Decisions An unelected “oversight committee” and “budget delegates” — not the elected Mayor or Council — assess, refine, and advance spending proposals to a binding vote.
citations.filed_by: Jason Williams, Taxpayers Association of Oregon

citations.quote: That’s real money, decided not by the elected Council after public hearings, but through a separate structure of an unelected “oversight committee,” unelected city staff, and unelected neighborhood “budget delegates” who advance proposals to a binding, citywide vote.
citations.filed_by: Jason Williams, Taxpayers Association of Oregon

citations.quote: This measure builds a second, parallel budget system. One that grows automatically every year, is exempt from normal budget tradeoffs, and gets locked into the City Charter, where it’s nearly impossible to undo if it doesn’t work.
citations.filed_by: Vikki Payne, Future Portland Action T Fund

filed_by: Jason Williams, Taxpayers Association of Oregon
Vikki Payne, Future Portland Action T Fund

against.text: Argument filed by Bob Weinstein: “Portlanders shouldn’t be locked into a permanent $16 million commitment by people unwilling to show their faces.”

citations.quote: Portlanders shouldn’t be locked into a permanent $16 million commitment by people unwilling to show their faces.

This isn’t a pilot program the City can end if it doesn’t work. It’s a permanent charter amendment requiring at least 2% of The printing of these arguments does not constitute an endorsement by M statements made M- discretionary spending every year, indefinitely.
citations.filed_by: Jason Williams, Taxpayers Association of Oregon

citations.quote: And because it’s in the charter, no future mayor or council could adjust it — no matter what needs or opportunity Portland faces.
citations.filed_by: Amy Ruiz, Protect Our City Services

citations.quote: No other city does participatory budgeting the way Measure 26-267 proposes. The Measure 26-267 campaign says participatory budgeting is proven elsewhere, citing New York, Boston, Paris, Seoul, and Mexico City. Here’s what they don’t tell you: not one of those cities — not one city anywhere — has done what this measure would do: permanently lock a mandatory budget set-aside into its charter.
citations.filed_by: Amy Ruiz, Protect Our City Services

filed_by: Jason Williams, Taxpayers Association of Oregon
Amy Ruiz, Protect Our City Services
